Three card treatments, real data, all five test items

Same real MenuItemCard data path, five real items chosen to include the weak photography on purpose: Kinder and Pistachio (the good photos) alongside Omelette, Cheddar Sauce, and Green Salad (plain, ordinary product shots). Same real prices from Supabase. Screenshots at 390px and 1024px.

Levers explored: photo share and crop, price as a typographic event, description removed entirely (lives on the detail page now), warm-tinted shadow for card-plane depth, add control as a real ≥44px object, popular badge as a designed shape.

Frame

Tall 4:5 photo, ribbon-cut popular badge, price in accent-colored display type in a compact footer, circular add button peeking at the seam between photo and footer, half on each.

Survives all 5 items, both widths

1024px

390px

Ledger

Slightly shorter photo, corner-cut popular badge flush in the photo corner, large price directly under the name, a full solid pill "+ Add" button spanning the card's width.

Survives all 5 items, both widths

1024px

390px

Stamp

Photo fills almost the entire card, name and price overlaid directly on a warm dark scrim at the bottom, circular add button floats on the photo itself.

Breaks: price gets clipped

1024px

390px

I'd pick Frame.

Stamp is ruled out, not a style preference, a real failure: name and price sit inline at the bottom of the photo competing for the same line, and the moment a name runs long ("Cheddar Sauce", "Pistachio") the price clips, "190 EG", "120 EG", visible at both 390 and 1024. Fixable in theory (stack name over price instead of inline) but that removes exactly what made Stamp distinct, so it's not really Stamp anymore at that point.

Frame over Ledger comes down to what "depth" means literally. Ledger is a clean stacked panel: photo, then a big price, then a big button, all flat rectangles in a column. Frame's add button actually occupies two planes at once, sitting on the photo and the footer simultaneously, which is a real z-axis composition, not just bigger type and a bigger button. That's closer to what was asked for: weight through scale and depth, not just scale. Both pass every hard constraint (44px+ targets, verified 48px on both; survives all five items including the plain ones; no description; warm shadow, not black).

Ledger is the safer fallback if an icon-only add control feels ambiguous next to an explicit "+ Add" label, that's a legitimate, real tradeoff, not a flaw in Ledger.
